title: Sliding window beats linear attention, but only on short answers
gist: A memory-matched distillation of Qwen3-4B-Instruct shows sliding window attention with sinks matches or beats a hybrid sliding-window + mLSTM ('Bifocal') layer on short answers, but Bifocal solves 1.8x as many long-answer AIME/HMMT problems at the same ~195 tokens/s decode speed. The author argues log-likelihood benchmarks cannot distinguish these architectures and stacked windows reach only ~1.5 windows effectively.

insights.claim: For Qwen3-4B each generated token uses about 144 KiB of KV cache, so a single 10,000-token reasoning answer needs about 1.4 GiB, which quickly exceeds GPU memory when serving many concurrent requests.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Reasoning-model serving is memory-bound, driving demand for HBM and for fixed-memory attention architectures.
insights.quote: For Qwen3-4B each token uses about 144 KiB, so one 10,000-token answer needs about 1.4 GiB.

insights.claim: There are two ways to keep attention memory fixed: forget old tokens via sliding window attention, or compress them into a fixed-size state via linear attention and gated successors such as Mamba, Gated DeltaNet and mLSTM.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Frames the architectural fork for efficient long-context inference.
insights.locator: There are two ways to keep memory fixed

insights.claim: When retrofitting a pretrained model, sliding window attention collapses once the initial tokens leave the window because heads use them to park spare probability mass; attention sinks (StreamingLLM pinned tokens or gpt-oss-style learned biases) fix this.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Attention sinks are a required ingredient for cheap SWA retrofits.

themes.theme: Benchmark blind spots in linearization research

insights.claim: The 'Sliding-window beats linear attention' paper shows a training-free 64-token window with four sink tokens recovers 99% of the teacher's score on six standard benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Standard benchmarks barely test long-range memory.

insights.claim: Many linearization papers report only log-likelihood benchmarks such as HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, ARC and MMLU, which cannot reveal whether a model remembers anything far back since a 64-token window recovers 99% on them.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Claims of efficient-architecture parity based on these benchmarks are unreliable for reasoning workloads.
insights.quote: If a 64-token window recovers 99% on them, they cannot tell you whether a model remembers anything far back.
insights.locator: The last point is a problem for the whole field.

insights.claim: Prior comparisons favoring sliding windows used linear models retrofitted on small budgets of 20 to 600 million tokens and 'long context' benchmarks with long inputs but short answers.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Conclusions from short-answer long-context benchmarks do not extend to long generation.

insights.claim: Averaging over all problems hides where a compressed state helps; architectures must be evaluated on long generations and broken down by answer length.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Evaluation methodology change needed to price efficient-attention trade-offs correctly.
insights.quote: Evaluate on long generations, and look at them by length.

insights.claim: The author distilled Qwen3-4B-Instruct into four students with identical memory of 576 cached tokens per layer, using the same 4.1-billion-token budget on sequences up to 40K tokens.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Provides a clean, equal-memory ablation rare in the literature.

insights.claim: Because an mLSTM recurrent state must be stored in FP32 to avoid drift, one 128x128 state costs as much memory as 128 BF16 cached tokens, and placing states on query heads rather than key-value heads costs four times as much under grouped-query attention.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Hidden memory costs of linear states must be counted when comparing architectures.

insights.claim: On short-answer benchmarks the SWA student beats Bifocal by 0.7 to 1.5 points, agreeing with the sliding-window paper that a larger window is as good as a state when answers are a few hundred tokens.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: For chat/short-answer workloads, plain SWA with sinks is sufficient.
insights.quote: On short answers, a larger window is as good as a state, or slightly better.
insights.locator: Sliding window alone is enough for short answers

insights.claim: On AIME and HMMT math, where answers average about 7,600 tokens, Bifocal averages 15.5% versus 13.8% for SWA, a gap at the edge of statistical significance (95% CI 0.0 to 3.4 points).
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Hybrid linear+window layers offer a modest edge for long reasoning.
insights.locator: The linear mixer helps on long answers

insights.claim: On the 96 long-answer math problems Bifocal solves 1.8 times as many as the SWA student, and produces 66 correct answers longer than 4,000 tokens versus 26 for SWA.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Long-generation reasoning is where compressed state pays off.
insights.quote: On the 96 with long answers, Bifocal solves 1.8 times as many
insights.locator: The linear mixer helps on long answers

insights.claim: Giving almost all memory to the linear mixer (64-token window plus per-query-head states) collapses math performance to 4.2% versus 15.5%, showing exact recall of the recent past remains essential.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Pure linear/recurrent architectures are not a drop-in replacement for attention.
insights.quote: Exact recall over the recent past is still essential, and a compressed state blurs that information.
insights.locator: A linear mixer alone is not enough either

insights.claim: The best design uses both: a window alone runs out on long answers and a linear mixer alone blurs the recent past, so Bifocal blends them via a per-head data-dependent sigmoid gate.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Hybrid attention layers are likely the direction for efficient reasoning models.

insights.claim: Although 36 stacked 576-token windows give a theoretical reach of 20,736 tokens, the effective range of stacked sliding windows is about 1.5 windows regardless of depth because a distant token's influence decays roughly exponentially across windows.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Undercuts the Longformer/Mistral argument that stacked SWA gives long-range attention.
insights.locator: Can't stacked sliding window layers see further?

insights.claim: Like CNNs, whose effective receptive field is a small fraction of the theoretical one, transformers keep most token signal on the residual path so only a fraction is relayed through each attention window, while a linear mixer's recurrent state carries earlier tokens forward directly.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Explains mechanistically why recurrent state helps long reasoning.
insights.locator: The reason is the same as for CNNs

insights.claim: In vLLM on an H100 with Qwen3.5-4B-shaped models, Bifocal and pure SWA both decode at about 195 tokens/s from 1K to 128K prompt tokens, within 2% of each other, while Qwen3.5's native GDN plus attention hybrid slows to 146 tokens/s and full attention to 92 tokens/s at 128K.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Fixed-memory layers roughly double long-context decode throughput versus full attention, improving serving economics.
insights.quote: both hold steady at about 195 tokens/s from 1K all the way to 128K prompt tokens
insights.locator: What does the linear mixer cost?

insights.claim: Bifocal's prefill runs at 63% to 83% of SWA's speed, taking 1.8 s instead of 1.5 s before the first token of a 128K prompt, which is negligible against nearly a minute to generate a 10,000-token answer.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Prefill penalty is minor for long-form reasoning workloads.
insights.locator: Where the linear mixer does cost time

insights.claim: Students were distilled via layer-wise hidden-state alignment (819M tokens) followed by KL-only logit distillation (3.28B tokens) on a Nemotron generalist data mix of 40% chat, 20% code, 20% math, 15% science and 5% safety.
insights.speaker: Lukas
insights.so_what: Cheap distillation (~4B tokens) can retrofit pretrained models into efficient architectures.
